text:
I really disagree, programming is not dead. Far from it, we need skilled practitioners and designers now more than ever. I discussed this detail in The Decoherence Trap, which was trending for a minute there, but another (quicker) thing I'd recommend reading is my AI usage policy's section on coding.

In short, if you don't aggressively create and maintain solid, well thought out abstraction layers that are human driven, and only use AI at the edges, you're going to find yourself in sleep walking into an unmaintainable mess sooner rather than later. We already struggled with decoherence and code maintainability prior to AI, and AI is only accelerating it.

I say this as an early adopter, having seen every strategy and idea play out. There simply is no way to prevent decoherence, and the faster and harder you push AI, the more decoherence it adds.

Anyways, take heart, there's going to be plenty of slop for us to clean up for a very long time.

"DDoS" doesn't mean "thing I don't like happening at scale." A DDoS is a specific technical attack; calling datacenter electricity demand a "DDoS on reality" is like calling your morning commute a "buffer overflow on the highway." It's the kind of metaphor that sounds incisive until you think about it for eight seconds. The actual concerns buried here, resource consumption, labor displacement, surveillance infrastructure, are real and worth discussing seriously, which is precisely why wrapping them in this breathless rhetoric is counterproductive. You can't analyze tradeoffs when everything is already at maximum alarm.

The political analysis is even weaker. "AI companies" apparently constitute a unified bloc of fascist collaborators, evidence for which includes: some executives attended an inauguration. The author knows this, which is why they pre-emptively dismiss open-weight models and local inference as corporate misdirection; a neat trick that makes the argument unfalsifiable.

Cost estimates. Something might be possible with an agent at a cost of hundreds of dollars, is that worthwhile?

The core skill in using these tools is the same as the skill you need when writing code by hand. You have to understand the given requirement, the shape of the solution, and how to verify that the code that was produced actually matches the intent. People who don't work with LLMs seem to have this naive idea that it's sort of like a slot machine where you put a query in and then you either get a correct result or some nonsense and you have to try again.

The way this process actually works is that you start by understanding the problem and figuring out how you want to solve it in terms of architecture, data structures, and algorithms that will be used. Then you get the LLM to come up with a rough shape of the solution, and iterate on it until it works the way you want.

There's so many different types of developer jobs. The thesis statement here is probably true for lots of them.

One type I've had where it's less true is doing exploratory greenfield product engineering in an early stage startup. You can automate or optimise some simple and time consuming business processes with a well-considered integration to a frontier model API. This has been the case long enough that the people with a few years of experience with it have a meaningful advantage in terms of job performance over someone who doesn't. You develop an intuition for which problems are and aren't tractable to that kind of solution, which models and effort levels to try, how to formulate prompts, the likely quality level of the results and so on. Often the "AI skill" is combining that experience with an awareness of what the business is doing and spotting the next automatable thing. Smaller startups always have more work than anyone can possibly do, so rather than putting anyone out of a job you're generally just giving someone more time for other things.

Some (but by no means all) employers are already beginning to filter for this kind of thing when hiring. It's a niche, but everyone's in one niche or another. text:
When I was first learning the C programming language, in my early 20s, it was common knowledge that of the two ways to increment a variable, i++ was slower than ++i. The post-increment function returned the original value of i, which meant stashing a copy of that value before performing the increment. Pre-increment avoided this wasteful operation.

And by “common knowledge” I really mean folklore, because I turned 20 in 1995 and even by then, the most basic of optimising compilers knew to check if you ever used the return value of i++, and if not, skip the operation to save it.


The folklore survives in C++, I think, at least for class-type iterators. With built-in integers and raw pointers the two forms compile to the same thing when the result is discarded. A user-defined postfix operator++(int) has to copy the old value and return it by value, though, while the prefix one increments in place and returns a reference. For trivial iterators like std::vector<T>::iterator an optimizer will usually erase the copy, and with optimization on you probably won't measure much, as this revisit of an old benchmark found. Debug builds are another story, which is why static analyzers like PVS-Studio still flag it++ where the result is unused. ++it costs nothing to type, so it stays my default.
